1. Cardiovascular risk (CVR) #2

Cardiovascular risk #3

  • Cardiovascular risk (CVR) = The probability to develop a CV disease in a time frame, depending on the influence of different CVR factors
  • The concept of cardiovascular risk is a notion linked to both the asymptomatic phases of atherosclerosis (in primary prevention) and the phases in which clinical manifestations are present, when we talk about secondary prevention (prevention of new cardiovascular events in people who already have a constituted cardiovascular pathology).

CV risk factors (CVRF) #4

  • Variables associated with an increased risk of disease, independently correlated to the subsequent occurrence of cardiovascular diseases.
  • Comparison between the risk of the exposed and the non-exposed to the risk factor.

Traditional CV risk factors #5

  • Modifiable risk factors
  • Unhealthy Lifestyle
  • Obesity
  • Hyperglycemia
  • High blood pressure
  • Increased LDL, decreased HDL cholesterol
  • Smoking
  • Unmodifiable risk factors
  • Male gender
  • Age (>45 in men and >55 in women)
  • Family history of premature CV diseases (<55 in men and <65 in women)

CV risk factors #6

  • Modifiable risk factors – unhealthy lifestyle (amplify the expression of other risk factors)
  • Hypercaloric diet
  • Diet rich in trans and saturated fats, red meat, refined sugars, rich in food with high glycemic index, salt
  • Sedentary lifestyle
  • Excessive alcohol consumption
  • Smoking

Cardiovascular risk estimation #7

  • Identification of individual cardiovascular risk factors
  • Cardiovascular risk assessment
  • Charts (e.g.) – SCORE
  • SCORE-2 and SCORE-2-OP risk charts for fatal and non-fatal (myocardial infarction, stroke) atherosclerosis (ASCVD)

Slide 8 #8

  • The current guidelines on CVD prevention in clinical practice concentrate principally on the risk factors, risk classification, and prevention of ASCVD, management.

SCORE-2 = Systematic Coronary Risk Estimation #9

  • SCORE-2-OP = Systematic Coronary Risk Estimation 2-Older Persons

Patient categories and associated cardiovascular disease risk. #10

APPLIED FOR PATIENTS WITHOUT CARDIOVASCULAR DISEASES #24

APPLIED FOR PATIENTS WITHOUT CARDIOVASCULAR DISEASES #25

Slide 26 #26

Atherosclerosis #27

  • - product of a slowly developing pathophysiological process in medium to large arteries.
  • - is a complex chronic inflammatory process which results in the formation of plaques in the artery wall which may restrict blood flow or may rupture and lead to thrombosis.
  • - chronic inflammatory disease of arteries initiated by lipid entry

Atherosclerosis #28

  • Atherosclerosis is a disease process which is triggered by physical or chemical insults to the endothelial cell layer of arteries.
  • The earliest event in atherogenesis is injury to the endothelium, which can be triggered by :
  • Physical injury or stress as a result of direct trauma or hypertension
  • Turbulent blood flow, for example, where arteries branch
  • Circulation of reactive oxygen species (free radicals), e.g., from smoking or air pollutants
  • Hyperlipidemia (high blood concentrations of LDL or VLDL)
  • Chronically elevated blood glucose levels
  • Homocysteinemia, which results from an inherited metabolic defect that leads to very high levels of the homocysteine,
  • .

Slide 29 #29

Slide 30 #30

  • The oxidized-LDLs induce the activation of endothelial cells and the expression of leukocyte adhesion molecules (such as VCAM1-vascular cell adhesion molecule 1)  monocyte adhesion to the endothelium  transmigration of monocytes into the intima, where they differentiate into macrophages
  • T lymphocytes join macrophages in the intima during plaque evolution
  • Macrophages  incorporat modified lipoproteins  become lipid-rich foam cells  the inflammatory response stimulates migration and replication of vascular smooth muscle cells  accumulate in the plaque to form a fibroproliferative lesion
  • the plaque - abnormal lipid metabolism  forming a necrotic core
  • Inflammatory response

Initiation of the atherosclerotic lesion. #31

  • The fatty streak phase of atherosclerosis begins with dysfunctional endothelial cells and the retention of apoB-containing lipoproteins (LDL, VLDL, and apoE remnants) in the subendothelial space.
  • Retained lipoproteins are modified (oxidation, glycation, enzymatic), which, along with other atherogenic factors, promotes activation of endothelial cells.
  • Activated endothelial cells have increased expression of monocyte interaction/adhesion molecules (selectins, VCAM-1) and chemoattractants (MCP-1) leading to attachment and transmigration of monocytes into the intimal space.
  • Activated endothelial cells also promote the recruitment of other immune cells including dendritic cells, mast cells, regulatory T (T-reg) cells, and T helper 1 (Th-1) cells.
  • The monocytes differentiate into macrophages and express receptors that mediate the internalization of VLDL, apoE remnants, and modified LDL to become foam cells. In addition, inflammatory signaling pathways are activated in macrophage foam cells leading to more cell recruitment and LDL modification.

Slide 32 #32

  • The vulnerable plaque results from an unresolved inflammatory status of the lesion foam cell core  causes thinning of the fibrous cap  prone to rupture exposing prothrombotic components to platelets and procoagulation factors leading to thrombus formation and clinical events.

Slide 34 #34

  • Primary prevention is defined as the totality of actions carried out in order to prevent the occurrence of cardiovascular diseases in people free of cardiovascular pathology.
  • 
  • Action on risk factors
  • Secondary prevention is defined as the totality of actions carried out in order to prevent new cardiovascular events in people who already have a cardiovascular disease.

CLINICAL MANAGEMENT OF THE CARDIOVASCULAR RISK #35

  • Optimal clinical management of cardiovascular risk should be multifactorial, intensive and started early.
  • It is achieved by multiple methods, targeting multiple objectives: lifestyle, obesity, blood pressure, diabetes, lipids,......
  • Lifestyle optimization through the anti-risk diet, moderate daily exercise and smoking cessation/ non-smoking status is mandatory to control all risk factors targeted by clinical management: hyperglycemia, hypertension, obesity, dyslipidemia, platelet control.

2. Dyslipidemia (DLP) #36

HYPERLIPIDEMIA #37

  • Increased serum cholesterol and/or triglycerides above normal range.
  • DYSLIPIDEMIA
  • Hyperlipidemia accompanied by low serum HDL-cholesterol
  • Dyslipidemias are metabolic abnormalities characterized by increases (hyperlipidemias) or decreases (hypolipidemias) in plasma lipids.
  • In practice, the term refers to hypercholesterolemia and/or hypertriglyceridemia, with/or without a decrease in HDL (expressed as HDL-cholesterol). Their importance derives from the association with the increased cardiovascular risk

Hyperlipidemia classification #38

  • Hypercholesterolemia
  • Hypertriglyceridemia
  • Mixed Hyperlipidemia
  • Hypo HDL-emia (isolated or associated with Hyperlipidemia)
  • European Association of Atherosclerosis

Slide 39 #39

  • Lipid therapeutic goals are the values we must achieve through treatment; they are strictly individualized according to the overall cardiovascular risk.
  • In the modern approach to dyslipidemias, the notion of therapeutic goal transcends in importance and practically replaces the notion of normal serum lipid values (or, in other words, each category of patients has certain "normal values" strictly individualized according to cardiovascular risk).

Slide 40 #40

  • Total Cholesterol (Col): serum total cholesterol level (esterified and free) within all lipoprotein classes.
  • High-density lipoprotein (HDL) cholesterol : cholesterol transported by HDL from tissues, including arteries, to the liver, having anti-atherogenic properties.
  • Low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol: cholesterol (mostly esterified) transported by LDL to the tissues, including arteries, being the predominant atherogenic lipoprotein
  • Can be calculated- Friedewald formula:
  • LDL = Total cholesterol- (HDL + TG / 5 (mg/dl))
  • Can only be calculated if TG <400 mg/dl.
  • Triglyceridemia (TG): serum triglyceride level within all lipoprotein classes.

Major Serum Lipoprotein Classes (LP) #41

  • LIPOPROTEINS
  • - biochemical assembly that contains both proteins and lipids
  • - transport lipids and cholesterol around the body in the blood.
  • Chylomicrons (chilo): - major transport form of triglycerides and exogenous cholesterol from intestines into blood.
  • VLDL (VeryLowDensity lipoprotein) – endogenous lipid transportation, especially TG to tissues.
  • IDL (intermediate density) – TG and cholesterol esters transportation; atherogenic role.
  • LDL – major transport form of cholesterol esters.
  • - low density and large particles- phenotype A
  • - high density and small particles- phenotype B, atherogenic
  • - intermediate phenotype
  • HDL – cholesterol transport from tissues, including arteries, towards the liver.
  • Intermediate lipoprotein forms ( chylomicron remnants and VLDL remnants, HDL 2 and 3)

Apoproteins (Apo): #42

  • Protein component of lipoproteins
  • -roles
  • structural (ensures lipoprotein macromolecule stability)
  • functional (binding to receptors and enzyme activity).
  • Apo B (in LDL) is the main atherogenic
  • Apo A (in HDL) is anti-atherogenic
  • Lipoprotein Lp (a) – role in atherogenesis and thrombogenesis
  • Fatty Acids (FA): involved in cholesterol esterification, hepatic and adipose tissue triglyceride and VLDL synthesis
  • Free FA -in the bloodstream bound to albumin

VLDL #43

  • Lipoproteins

Slide 44 #44

Slide 45 #45

Reference values #46

  • Total serum cholesterol <190 mg/dl (<5 mmol/l)
  • Serum triglycerides <150 mg/dl
  • HDL-cholesterol >40 mg/dl (>1 mmol/) in men and >50 mg/dl (1,2 mmol/l) in women
  • Normal values are referred to as mean statistic population values, corresponding to the lowest cardiovascular morbidity and mortality.
  • * Conversion factor for cholesterol: 1mmol = 38,6 mg
  • * Conversion factor for TG: 1mmol = 88,6 mg

Clinical types of dyslipidemias #47

POLYGENIC HYPERCHOLESTEROLEMIA #48

  • the most common cause of elevated serum cholesterol concentrations (1:250 persons), caused by:
  • genotype (multiple genes)
  • aggravated by lifestyle factors.
  • needs exclusion of other hypercholesterolemia causes
  • - usually moderate increase in cholesterol level;
  • - usually found in people with:
  • family history of CVD,
  • arcus cornealis,
  • xanthelasma

FAMILIAL HYPERCHOLESTEROLEMIA #49

  • Genetic disorder caused by an autosomal dominant mutation of LDL-receptors (loss of function of LDL gene receptor or ApoB gene or gain of function of PCSK9), inducing an increased CV Risk, even without having further risk factors.
  • Heterozygous forms, usually common finding (1:500):
  • severe hypercholesterolemia in adults;
  • premature onset of CVD;
  • 20-fold increased risk of myocardial infarction in men;
  • 6-fold increased CV risk in women;
  • early development of coronary atheromas (17 years);
  • tendinous xanthomas, tuberous, arcus cornealis, xanthelasma, including in first degree relatives.

Slide 50 #50

  • Familial hypercholesterolemiaHomozygous forms –less frequent (1:1.000.000) and accompanied by a very high CV Risk - Severe CVD occurs in young patients -below 20 years.Clinical findings:- severe hypercholesterolemia, over 500 mg/dl;- tendinous xanthoma, tuberous, arcus cornealis, xanthelasma;- family history of early CVD;- hypercholesterolemia (> 300 mg/dl) in first degree relatives

Definition of hypertriglyceridaemia #51

  • According to the European Atherosclerosis Society consensus document:
  • mild to moderate HTG
  • 150 mg/dl (1.7 mmol/L) – 880 mg/dl (10 mmol/L)
  • Severe
  • > 880 mg/dl
  • Severe HTG is associated with an increased risk for pancreatitis.

HYPERTRIGLYCERIDEMIA #52

  • Primary genetically determined forms are autosomal dominant (1:600).
  • Clinical findings:
  • - hypertriglyceridemia > 500 mg/dl;
  • - lipaemia retinalis, eruptive xanthomas, hepatosplenomegaly;
  • - increased risk of pancreatitis.
  • Secondary forms:
  • (1) increased alcohol consumption
  • (2) diabetes mellitus
  • (3) renal failure

Slide 53 #53

Mixed hyperlipidemia #54

  • A less common cause, but severe, of early CVD, peripheral artery disease, carotid atherosclerosis.
  • Primary forms - polygenic and autosomal dominant
  • Secondary forms - frequently associated with obesity and metabolic syndrome, hypothyroidism, diabetes
  • Clinical findings:
  • - Hypercholesterolemia > 300 mg/dl (8-12 mmol/l);
  • - Hypertriglyceridemia > 500 mg/dl (8-12 mmol/l);
  • - palms and elbows xanthomas;

Familial combined hyperlipidaemia (FCH) #55

  • Familial combined hyperlipidaemia (FCH) is a highly prevalent dyslipidaemia (1:100) and an important cause of premature CAD.
  • FCH is characterized by elevated levels of LDL-C, TGs or both.
  • The phenotype varies even among members of the same family.
  • FCH shares considerable phenotype overlap with type 2 diabetes and MetS.
  • FCH is a complex disease and the phenotype is determined by interaction of multiple susceptibility genes and the environment.

Atherogenic dyslipidemia – Atherogenic triad #56

  •  HDL-C
  • ± LDL
  • Small
  • Dense
  •  TG
  • Metabolic syndrome
  • T2DM
  •  60 % CVD-ATS

Notes: SLIDE 2: ATHEROGENIC LIPOPROTEIN PROFILE The lipid profile of patients with type 2 diabetes and of those with the Metabolic Syndrome (MetS) is characterized by the concurrent presence of qualitative as well as quantitative lipoprotein abnormalities: low levels of HDL-C (<50 mg/dl in women, < 40 mg/dl in men), increased triglycerides (TG >150 mg/dl), and prevalence of LDL particles that are smaller and denser than normal. This lipid phenotype has been defined as Atherogenic Lipoprotein Profile (1). Interestingly, elevated LDL-C level is not typical of type 2 diabetes nor MetS. This lipid phenotype is also present in women with Polycystic Ovarian Syndrome (POS) and is a feature of the most common genetic form of dyslipidemia: Familial Combined Hyperlipidemia (FCHL) REFERENCES 1 Austin MA, Breslow JL, Hennekens CH, Buring JE, Willett WC, Krauss RM. Low-density lipoprotein subclass patterns and risk of myocardial infarction. JAMA. 1988;260:1917-1921.

Atherogenic dyslipidemia – Atherogenic triad #57

  • Inflammation, atherosclerosis/ CV disease
  • These metabolic changes, coupled with the pro-oxidative, proinflammatory and prothrombotic state of insulin resistance, predispose to the development of accelerated atherogenesis in ‘cardiometabolic’ patients.

Atherogenic dyslipidemia #58

  • Metabolic syndrome
  • T2 DM
  • Insulin resistance
  • Total Cholesterol and LDL  might be normal
  • High TG level
  • Low HDL
  • Low ApoA-1
  • LDL : small, dense, atherogenic particles
  • High ApoB-100
  • Extended postprandial hyperlipemia
  • VLDL, IDL and Chylo remnants rich in cholesterol esters, uptake by macrophages;

SECONDARY HYPERLIPIDEMIAS: #59

  • Hypercholesterolemia:
  • - Hypothyroidism
  • - Cholestasis
  • - Nephrotic syndrome
  • - Porphyria
  • - Pregnancy
  • - Thiazides and progesterone
  • - Post renal transplantation
  • Mixed Hyperlipidemia:
  • - Uncontrolled diabetes mellitus
  • - Nephrotic syndrome
  • - Chronic Renal Failure
  • - Thiazides, steroids, retinoids, progesteronic drugs
  • Hypertriglyceridemia:
  • - Uncontrolled diabetes mellitus
  • - Nephrotic syndrome
  • - Chronic Renal Failure
  • - Thiazides, steroids, cyclosporine, retinoids, progesterone, estrogenic drugs

Biological impact of dyslipidemias #60

Biological impact- Cardiovascular risk #61

  • Hypercholesterolemia is a major and independent risk factor for coronary heart disease (CHD)
  • The risk is continuous, there is no protective threshold; it begins at values above 150 mg/dl, moderately increasing up to 250 mg/dl, and extremely increasing above this value.
  • LDL
  • colest

LDL - as the primary driver of atherogenesis #63

  • There is incontrovertible evidence that LDL is causal for ASCVD.
  • Jan Boren et al.

Reduction in LDL – reduction in CV events #64

  • CV, cardiovascular; BCV, boală coronariană vasculară; LDL-C, colesterol lipoproteină de densitate micăFerence BA, et al. Eur Heart J 2017;38(32):2459–2472
  • Reducerea proporțională a riscului CV , %
  • Reducerea LDL-C, mmol/L
  • “the lower the better”
  • “the earlier the better”
  • “the longer the better”

Notes: Reference Ference BA, Ginsberg HN, Graham I, et al. Low-density lipoproteins cause atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease. 1. Evidence from genetic, epidemiologic, and clinical studies. A consensus statement from the European Atherosclerosis Society Consensus Panel. Eur Heart J 2017;38(32):2459–2472

Frank L.J. Visseren et al. #65

  • HDL decrease is a significant and independent predictor for CHD for values
  • < 40mg/dl in men
  • < 50 mg/dl in women
  • Reverse cholesterol transport
  • Antiinfectious activity
  • Antithrombotic activity
  • Anti-

  • Antiapoptotic activity

  • HDL-antiatherogenic effect

Hypertriglyceridemia impact #67

  • Mild and moderate forms – predictive for the development of coronary heart disease
  • Severe forms (>880 mg/dl) – risk factor for acute pancreatitis

Risk factors for dyslipidemias #69

Hyperlipidemia/Dyslipidemia risk factors #70

  • 1. UNHEALTHY LIFESTYLE:
  • • High caloric intake, animal lipids (saturated), „trans” FA and refined sugars;
  • • Increased alcohol intake> 30gr/day;
  • • Smoking;
  • • Sedentary lifestyle;
  • • Psycho-social stress;
  • 2. GENETIC FACTORS (familial forms)
  • 3. METABOLIC SYNDROME

Low - HDL additional risk factors #71

  • • Abdominal obesity or within the metabolic syndrome
  • • Uncontrolled diabetes mellitus
  • • Chronic renal failure
  • • Non-selective beta-blockers, thiazides, progesteronic drugs
  • Smoking

Practical approach of dyslipidemias #72

Screening for dyslipidemia #73

  • ESC. Dyslipidemia guideline 2019. European Heart Journal 2019
Immediately irrespective of age, in persons with Conditions associated with high or very high CV risk (CVD, diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease, systemic inflammatory diseases, gestational diabetes or hypertension, erectile disfunction, etc) Clinical signs suggestive for a genetic for of dyslipidemia (xantoma, xantelasma, arcus cornealis <45 years of age)
In apparently healthy persons staring from the age of 40 in men and 50 (or post-menopausal) in women
Relatives of patients with severe forms of dyslipidemia
Relatives of patients with premature CVD (defined as CVD below the age of 55 in men and <65 in women)

Notes: Momentul şi modalitatea prin care se recomandă screening-ul pentru depistarea dislipidemiilor depind de mai mulţi factori.

Treatment targets and goals for CVD prevention #76

Lipid treatment goals
LDL-C is the primary goalVery CVR high: LDL-C <55 mg/dl AND decrease with ≥50% from baseline level
High CVR: LDL-C <70 mg/dl AND decrease with ≥50% from baseline level
Moderate CVR: LDL-C <100 mg/dl
Low CVR: LDL-C <116 mg/dl
HDL-CThere are no recommendations, but values < 40 mg/dl in men and <50 mg/dl in women are associated with increased CVD risk
TGThere are no goals; but levels < 150 mg/dl are associated with lower CVD risk. At levels >150 mg/dl screening for additional risk factors should be performed TG ≥880 mg/dl – immediate initiation of therapy for decreasing the risk of acute pancreatitis

Therapy of Dyslipidemia #78

  • Lifestyle changes
  • Diet
  • Physical exercise
  • Smoking cessation
  • Specific pharmacoteraphy

Slide 79 #79

Food choices to lower LDL-cholesterol and improve lipid profile #80

  • ESC. Dyslipidemia guideline 2019. European Heart Journal 2019

Dietary lipids #81

Regulation of the main lipid metabolic pathways- Diet #82

  • Hypocaloric diets with reduced cholesterol intake (< 300 mg/day), monounsaturated and „cis” polyunsaturated lipids reduce cholesterolemia and triglyceridemia, increasing HDL-chol level.
  • Dietary fibers induce the same changes.
  • Alcohol consumption < 30g/day increases HDL-chol

Regulation of the main lipid metabolic pathways- Diet #83

  • Dietary lipids
  • - Saturated lipids- increase Cholesterol and TG and HDL-cholesterol.
  • - „trans” fat- the same effect as saturated lipids + lower HDL-chol
  • Dietary cholesterol – moderate effect on cholesterolemia (maximum 20% of the serum cholesterol levels).
  • High energy intake - obesity, which:
  • - stimulates VLDL-TG synthesis in the liver;
  • - lowers HDL-chol.
  • Alcohol: - increased synthesis and secretion of VLDL-TG

Slide 84 #84

Sources of trans fats (industrially hydrogenated) #85

  • commercial baked goods
  • crackers
  • cookies
  • cakes
  • fried foods
  • doughnuts
  • french fries
  • Regular
  • margarine

Negative aspects of trans fats obtained by industrial hydrogenation #86

  • Increase:
  • LDL- cholesterol and tryglicerides
  • Decrease HDL-cholesterol
  • Insulin resistance
  • Type 2 diabetes
  • Cancer risks
  • Weight gain and abdominal fat
  • Liver disfunction
  • Infertility
  • Pro-atherogenic effect: endothelial dysfunction, systemic inflammation, oxidative stress
  • Risk of coronary hearth disease and sudden death
  • Asthma
  • Displace EFAs (essential fatty Acids) in human milk affecting infant growth and development.

Saturated fats #87

  • Have important metabolic functions but they are not essential.
  • Are asociated with:
  • Increases in total cholesterol, LDL, and TG
  • Increases of HDL cholesterol
  • Daily recommended intake <10% of total caloric intake
  • Dietary sources:
  • Animal products (milk and milk products, meat, animal fat)
  • Coconut and palm tree oil
  • Negative effects
  • Are associated with an increased risk of CVD
  • However, just reducing the saturated fats will not cut down the risk. An important factor what they are replaced with. The most favourable effects are obtained by replacing saturated fats with cis-PUFA.

Add skim or low-fat milk to recipes instead of whole milk #88

  • Avoid salad dressings. Lemon juice & oils made of monounsaturated fats such as olive oil.
  • Try low-fat yogurt or cottage cheese in place of sour cream and mayonnaise
  • Use olive oil when cooking instead of butter, lard or stick margarines.
  • Bake, boil or steam vegetables.
  • Bake, boil, roast or simmer fish, meat and poultry.
  • Snack on fruits and vegetables such as carrots rather than cakes and ice cream
  • Do not eat fast food or pizza more than once weekly.
  • To cut down on Saturated Fats

Cut visible fat of the meat #89

  • Choose lean meats.
  • Cook with a nonstick pan to prevent the need for added fat during preparation.
  • Drain fat from meat or poultry by cooking them on a rack.
  • Flavor foods with spices and herbs instead of butter, margarine and sauces.
  • Limit consumption of fried foods, frozen and processed foods.
  • Remove skin from poultry prior to consumption.
  • Snack on popcorn and low-sodium pretzels rather than potato chips.
  • Check the nutrition facts labels on packaged foods. Choose items low in saturated fats.
  • To cut down on Saturated Fats

Unsaturated fats #90

  • Omega3, Omega-6 and mono-unsaturated fatty acids
  • Positive effects (summary)
  • decrease total cholesterol, LDL- cholesterol, TG.
  • prevent fatty deposits (plaques) in the arteries=> reduce the risk of heart disease and stroke.
  • lower blood pressure levels
  • reduce the risk of arrhythmia

Omega 3 Fatty Acids #91

  • Alpha-linolenic acid (ALA)
  • Eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA)
  • Docosahexaenoic acid (DHA)
  • Sources of Omega-3
  • Fat fish: herring, salmon, mackerel
  • Linseed, rapeseed, nuts, soybeans, avocado, corn oil
  • Marine algae (microalgae Crypthecodinium cohnii and Schizochytrium)

Benefits of Omega-3s #92

  • Anti-inflammatory
  • Lower triglyceride and cholesterol levels
  • Cancer prevention
  • Renal maintenance
  • Increase insulin sensitivity
  • Enhance thermogenesis and lipid metabolism
  • Benefits vision and brain function
  • Decrease skin inflammation
  • Inhibit platelet adhesion

Omega-6 fatty acids #93

  • Food sources
  • Vegetable oils: sunflower, corn, canola, grape seed, olive oil
  • Soy bean, hazelnut, avocado
  • Meat, eggs (arachidonic acid)
  • Effects
  • At the level of the vascular endothelium they have anti-inflammatory effect (positive effect on the pathogenetic pathways of atherosclerosis).
  • Replacing 1% of the energy intake from saturated fats with Omega-6 is associated with 2.0 mg/dl reduction of LDL-cholesterol and total cholesterol.
  • Reduction of triglycerides.
  • Slight reduction effect of HDL-cholesterol.

Mono-unsaturated fatty acids #94

  • Food sources
  • Avocado, nuts, hazelnuts
  • Olive oil, canola, corn, sunflower, grape seed
  • Animal foods (dairy products, eggs, meat, fish)
  • 20% of the energy intake should come from MUFA
  • Beneficial effects:
  • CVD risk reduction
  • Reduction of LDL-cholesterol (replacement of 1% energy from lipids saturated with MUFA determines the reduction of LDL cholesterol by 1.6 mg / dL)
  • Source of MUFA is important. The beneficial effects does not occur if the MUFA are of animal origin.
  • Schwingshackl L, et al. Lipids Health Dis. 2014;13:154

Physical exercise #95

  • Helps maintain energy balance and stimulates lipoprotein lipase activity, inducing:
  • - lowering triglyceridemia (VLDL)
  • - increasing HDL-Chol;
  • - moderate cholesterol reduction (LDL).
  • ESC. Dyslipidemia guideline 2019. European Heart Journal 2019

Pharmacotherapy for LDL-cholesterol #96

  • Statins – first line therapy, with titration to the maximum tolerated dose
  • Ezetimibe
  • monotherapy if statins are not tolerated
  • add-on therapy to statins if targets are not achieved with maximum tolerated statin dose
  • PCSK-9 inhibitors
  • Add-on to statins and ezetimibe if target not achieved with these (primary, secondary prevention and FH)
  • Add-on to ezetimibe in those with intolerance to statins

Statin mechanism of action #98

  • Mechanism of action
  • Reduce the synthesis of cholesterol in the liver by competitively inhibiting the enzyme HMG-CoA reductase, the rate-limiting step in cholesterol biosynthesis.
  • The reduction in intracellular cholesterol promotes increased LDL receptor (LDLR) expression at the surface of the hepatocytes, which in turn results in increased uptake of LDL from the blood.
  • Pleiotropic effects:
  • • inhibition of atherogenic mechanisms
  • • stabilization of atherosclerotic plaques
  • • improvement of endothelial dysfunction
  • • anti-thrombotic
  • anti - inflammatory

Ezetimibe #100

  • Inhibits intestinal uptake of dietary and biliary cholesterol at the level of the brush border of the intestine [by interacting with the Niemann-Pick C1-like protein 1 (NPC1L1)] without affecting the absorption of fat-soluble nutrients.
  • Dozes: 10 mg/day

PCSK9 inhibitors #101

  • New class of drugs that have been shown to dramatically lower LDL cholesterol levels.
  • PCSK9 inhibitors are monoclonal antibodies (MABs),
  • They inactivate a protein in the liver called proprotein convertase subtilisin kexin 9 (PCSK9).
  • PCSK9 itself inactivates the receptors on the liver cell surface that transport LDL into the liver for metabolism (break down). Without these receptors, more LDL remains in the blood.
  • That inactivation results in decreased LDL-receptor degradation, increased recirculation of the receptor to the surface of hepatocytes, and consequent lowering of LDL cholesterol levels in the bloodstream.
  • So, by inactivating PCSK9 via inhibition, more receptors are available to capture LDL for metabolism and removal from the blood.
  • Approved
  • evolocumab (Repatha)
  • alirocumab (Praluent)

Inclisiran #102

  • is a first-in-class, subcutaneously administered, small interfering RNA (siRNA) that prevents hepatic synthesis of proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9 (PCSK9), thereby decreasing circulating low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C)
  • causes a reduction in LDL-C concentrations by approximately 50% compared to placebo

Pharmacotherapy for hypertriglyceridemia #103

  • TG >880 mg/dl
  • therapy with fibrates, no alcohol consumption and severe hypolipidic diet
  • n-3 PUFA or nicotinic acid may be added to fibrates
  • High CV risk patients with TG>200 mg/dl
  • Statin is the first line therapy
  • In those with LDL within target, fenofibrate or n-3 PUFA may be added to statins
